title: Pyxis Cloud GPU Onramp Scouting Call
summary: Introductory partner-discovery between Redwood AE/SE and Pyxis Cloud to assess fit for a GPU onramp integration. Cover current infra, scale/timeline, security/compliance gating (SOC2, KMS, SSO), and initial pilot/benchmark plan. Agreed next steps: share security pack, pilot pricing, and schedule hands-on pilot in early September.
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployments
VPC/private control plane and KMS integration
transcript:
00:00 Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for making time, really excited to meet Pyxis. I’m Maya, AE on the Redwood side, with Carlos, our solutions engineer. Quick roll call?
00:08 Lina: Hi Maya, Lina here, Head of Platform at Pyxis. Noah is on from SRE, and Aisha from procurement.
00:15 Maya: Awesome. Real quick agenda — we want to understand your stack, goals for GPU onramp, constraints, and then surface what a pilot could look like. 
00:28 Carlos: Hi all — I’ll mostly focus on topology questions and what metrics matter for you. Feel free to interrupt — I talk fast.
00:35 Noah: Totally fine. Quick note — our timings are PST. Also we got an invite with a short questionnaire, sorry if some answers were a bit terse.
00:42 Maya: No worries. Lina, can you give a quick baseline: what do you run today for model serving and what’s the expected scale?
00:52 Lina: Sure. We run a mix — in prod we have model endpoints on our own k8s clusters with NVidia A100 and some T4s in a separate pool. Most inference is internal search and a customer-facing summarization microservice. Peak concurrent requests are around 1.2k qps across clusters, but bursty — like daily spikes during customer syncs.
01:12 Carlos: Got it. Are those endpoints autoscaled? And are you using any inference runtime like Triton or custom TF/PyTorch servers?
01:20 Lina: We use a custom PyTorch server with a small amount of Triton for specific models. Autoscaling is k8s HPA but it’s reactive and not great for sub-second tail latency needs.
01:32 Maya: Makes sense — typical. For context, Redwood can offer hosted endpoints or a dedicated GPU pool that you can reserve. We also do Private deployments (VPC) if you need control plane separation. What’s the main constraint pushing you to talk to partners like us?
01:48 Lina: Cost predictability and the ability to handle bursts without overprovisioning. Also data residency — some customers require that inference never leaves certain regions. 
01:58 Noah: Plus tighter key management; we have a customer audit roadmap: SOC2 Type II next Q and we need KMS integration and better audit logs.
02:10 Carlos: Understood. We support KMS (customer-managed keys), HSM integrations in Private, and we emit per-request audit logs that can be shipped to your SIEM. There might be some differences in log retention across Hosted vs Private.
02:24 Aisha: On procurement, we need to understand contract model — is pricing usage-based, committed reserved, or both? And what’s the minimum commitment for Dedicated pools?
02:34 Maya: We offer usage-based hosted pricing and reserved committed capacity for Dedicated. Minimums vary by region and GPU class; we’ll share a pricing sheet. For pilots most customers start with a short reserved pilot or low-commit burst capacity.
02:46 Lina: If we do a pilot, we want to validate cost-per-token and tail latency at 99.9 percentile not just average. Real customers notice spikes.
02:56 Carlos: Good point. For benchmarks we recommend a mixed workload: steady baseline and 3x burst patterns. We can provide a benchmark harness (scripts + sample traces) so you can run locally or we can run on Redwood lab infra.
03:12 Noah: Would the harness measure KV cache effectiveness? Our models rely heavily on prefix reuse.
03:18 Carlos: Yes, we capture prefix/KV cache hit rates, batching behavior, and per-token compute. Our runtime has smart KV cache and continuous batching — helps reduce cost in many workloads.
03:28 Lina: Are there any gotchas with quantized models? Some of our LLMs are in 4-bit quant and we get different perf profiles.
03:36 Carlos: We do a model onboarding pass — we test quantized variants and select best kernels. Sometimes 4-bit runs great, sometimes it changes latency SLO tradeoffs. We’ll include quantization notes in the onboarding doc.
03:49 Maya: On security, Noah mentioned SOC2. Are you asking Redwood to be SOC2 compliant or to provide artifacts for your vendor audit?
03:58 Noah: Both. Ideally Redwood would have SOC2 but if not, we need a security pack: architecture diagram, controls, encryption at-rest/in-transit details, KMS integration, and an incident response playbook.
04:12 Carlos: We have a security pack and an auditor-friendly kit. I’ll attach that link — note: we redact customer-specific stuff — but it includes process for Private deployments and on-prem references.
04:24 Aisha: Also SSO — we require SAML single sign-on and SCIM provisioning for RBAC.
04:30 Maya: Supported. We offer SAML SSO, SCIM, and role-based access controls. Private can enforce VPC peering and control plane isolation.
04:38 Lina: Network — do you support allowing egress only to our VPC for model artifacts or will outgoing IPs be dynamic?
04:46 Carlos: In Private we can lock to your VPC and egress is managed by your routing. For hosted we offer VPC peering and dedicated egress ranges, but that depends on region and partner datacenter. We’ll flag that as a checklist item.
04:58 Lina: Great. Timeline — we’re aiming to decide vendor and start pilot in the first two weeks of September. Is that feasible?
05:06 Maya: Yes — we can scope a 2–4 week pilot. Typical pilot activities: onboarding, running benchmark harness, cost analysis, and a short integration test with your app.
05:17 Noah: Who from Redwood would run the pilot? We’ll need SE time.
05:21 Carlos: I’ll lead the technical run and partner with our onboarding team. We’ll need access to traces and a sample model or container image (or we can run using our model copy if licensing allows).
05:33 Aisha: From procurement, we’ll need a short MSA and an SLA for latency/uptime during pilot.
05:40 Maya: We can provide a pilot MSA and a temporary SLA. I’ll have legal draft a short-term addendum.
05:47 Lina: Curious — are there competitors you see in this space that we should be aware of?
05:52 Maya: Common alternatives are self-hosting with CloudForge managed offerings, or AquilaAI’s hosted endpoints. We can go over tradeoffs in the follow-up.
06:03 Noah: On metrics — please include token cost breakdown, GPU utilization, and 99th/99.9th latency in the pilot deliverables.
06:10 Carlos: Noted. Also we'll instrument tracing hooks so you can correlate requests to latency buckets.
06:16 Maya: Few more quick questions — do you have hard constraints for data residency or encryption-at-rest keys staying in your KMS?
06:24 Lina: Some enterprise customers require the KMS to be under their tenancy — basically customer-managed keys that never leave their control.
06:32 Carlos: Private deployment supports that; we install the control plane in your VPC and use your KMS endpoints. Hosted can do BYOK in certain regions but there are extra steps.
06:44 Noah: Any limitations around GPU models in Private? We prefer A100 for throughput but also want lower-cost T4 for some lower-priority workloads.

Aisha Rahman: Share procurement timeline and standard MSA requirements (due 2025-08-30)

Schedule a hands-on pilot kickoff (target week of 2025-09-08)
Customer to provide traces + model access for benchmark
